ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics approval was obtained from the University of Western Australia Human Research Ethics Committee (RA/4/20/6423).

Participants were randomly assigned to either listen to a misleading AI-generated podcast segment, read a misleading AI-generated article, or listen to a neutral nondeceptive AI-generated podcast segment, and they were told that the materials were AI-generated.
We recruited 501 Prolific (http://www.prolific.com/) users from the United States, who indicated English fluency and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.
table.formatted: We recruited 501 Prolific (<ref type="url" target="http://www.prolific.com/">www.prolific.com</ref>) users from the United States, who indicated English fluency and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions, constrained only by approximately equal group sizes.
Participants were made aware of the article's AI source by two bold-font statements in the survey instructions stating ChatGPT to be the author.
That is, participants were asked to imagine themselves as an unscrupulous lobbyist paid to push some flawed position.
Participants completed three questionnaires.
Participants first received an ethics-approved information page, provided informed consent via tick box, and indicated their age and gender.

An audio-check question was added to help ensure participants were able to listen to the podcast, and encoding questions were added to measure participants' engagement with materials (see Questionnaires below for details).
Prolific inclusion criteria were also identical except for the requirement that participants have at least 10 previously completed studies on the platform.
We recruited 550 Prolific users from the United States.
Participants were made aware of the article's AI source.

More specifically, like the original activity, participants were asked to imagine themselves as an unscrupulous lobbyist paid to push some flawed position; then they were asked to identify, for two flawed positions, which of three AI prompts would best produce biased information supporting each flawed position.

However, before choosing prompts in the new activity, participants were asked to choose: (i) which of three arguments they wanted to use (e.g., the health benefits of drinking lemon water), and (ii) which of two manipulation techniques they wanted to use (e.g., appeals to authority); this gave 18 (3 × 2 × 3) possible topic-technique-prompt configurations.

In addition to the questionnaires used in Experiment 1, we firstly added a multiplechoice audio-check question with ten response options that could only be answered if the participant had audio enabled (i.e., "Select the correct response [i.e., colour] given in the audio clip."); this helped to ensure that participants listened to the podcast.

However, another simple explanation could be that participants paid more attention to the article, as reading the article was quicker and less amenable to multitasking; this explanation may be unlikely though, since we excluded those with poor performance on encoding checks in Experiment 2.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007), an a priori power analysis suggested a sample size of 100 participants per experimental condition to detect a small difference between two conditions (f = 0.2, α = .05, and 1 -β = .80). We recruited 501 Prolific (http://www.prolific.com/) users from the United States, who indicated English fluency and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%. Participants were randomly assigned to conditions, constrained only by approximately equal group sizes. Average age was M = 46.44 years (SD = 13.60, range 20-83), with 218 men, 276 women, and 6 non-binary participants. Participants' data were excluded if they: indicated inadequate effort (see Materials; n = 1); demonstrated an upwardly outlying (following the 2.2 interquartile-range rule) mean difference score between normal and reverse-coded belief questions (indicating uniform responding; n = 28) or an upwardly outlying response SD for belief and trust questions (indicative of erratic responding; n = 0); or had a completion time longer than four hours (n = 0). These exclusions left a final sample size of N = 472.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: AI-Podcast Misinformation: Testing Active versus Passive Inoculations
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Our first hypothesis is that trust in AI-generated information will be reduced by both passive and active inoculation (H1a/b), with a stronger effect for active inoculation (H2). We further hypothesise that beliefs will be influenced by AI-generated misinformation in both the written format (H3a) and audio-podcast format (H3b), with a stronger effect for the audio format (H4). Next, we hypothesise that the impact of the misleading podcast will be reduced by both passive inoculation (H5a) and active inoculation (H5b) with a stronger effect for active inoculation (H6). Lastly, we anticipate that misinformation effects will continue to influence belief following both inoculations (H7a/b; i.e., a continued influence effect).
table.design_dependent_variables: There will be two dependent variables and one covariate measure. Trust in AI-generated information will be measured by endorsement of seven statements (e.g., “AI-generated content is objective”) on an 11-point rating scale ranging from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), with two reverse-coded items. Misled beliefs will be measured by five statements (e.g., “Microwave radiation can create harmful chemicals in foods.”) on the same 11-point rating scale, with two reverse-coded items. Previous AI usage will be measured with three questions: the first will ask if participants have used generative AI tools in the past; if yes, the second will ask if they are familiar with Wondercraft or Gemini Notebook(LM) and their outputs; finally, the third will ask how often they have used AI for ten specific purposes (e.g., “For fun or entertainment”) on a five-point Likert scale (never, a few times a year, a few times a month, a few times a week, daily). However, only the second question (dummy coded) and two of the third question’s purposes relevant to learning (i.e., “To search for information or learn about something”; “To get advice on something”) will be used as measures of familiarity with the AI-podcast tools and previous AI use, respectively.
table.study_design_overview: One-way between-subjects design with five levels (control, misleading-article-only, misleading-podcast-only, misleading-podcast + passive inoculation, misleading-podcast + active inoculation), giving five total conditions that participants will be randomly assigned to using approximately equal cell sizes as the only constraint.
table.statistical_tests: To assess the effects of both misinformation and inoculation, we will perform one-way between-subjects ANOVAs with each dependent variable, using age or learning-relevant, previous-AI-use as covariates if significant correlations are found with them. Significant ANOVA results will be followed-up with hypothesis-based planned contrasts.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: To be included, participants on Prolific will have to have English fluency and have completed at least 10 previous studies with an overall approval rating of at least 98%. Datasets will be excluded if participants: indicate via an in-survey question that they were distracted while completing, or did not engage with, the experimental materials; demonstrate inadequate engagement with materials by answering every encoding question incorrectly; demonstrate, based on the 2.2 interquartile-range rule, either an upwardly outlying mean difference between normal and reverse-coded items or an upwardly outlying response SD for any question sets (indicative of erratic responding); or take longer than four hours to complete the study once opening it on Qualtrics. Further, participants familiar with NotebookLM were excluded in Experiment 1, as familiarity had a negative correlation with belief scores exclusively in the misleading-podcast-only condition; therefore, the same procedure will be implemented in this experiment if the same pattern repeats. If, however, an unexpectedly substantial number of participants are excluded, we will incrementally relax these criteria to regain experimental power without introducing significant bias.
table.sample_size: An a-priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) recommends a sample size of approximately 100 participants per experimental condition to detect a small difference between two between-subjects conditions (ƒ = .20, α = .05, 1 – β = .80). We will oversample this by 10% to account for potential exclusions.

Lastly, we anticipate that misinformation effects will continue to influence belief following both inoculations (H7a/b; i.e., a continued influence effect).", "There will be two dependent variables and one covariate measure. Trust in AI-generated information will be measured by endorsement of seven statements (e.g., “AI-generated content is objective”) on an 11-point rating scale ranging from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), with two reverse-coded items. Misled beliefs will be measured by five statements (e.g., “Microwave radiation can create harmful chemicals in foods.”) on the same 11-point rating scale, with two reverse-coded items. Previous AI usage will be measured with three questions: the first will ask if participants have used generative AI tools in the past; if yes, the second will ask if they are familiar with Wondercraft or Gemini Notebook(LM) and their outputs; finally, the third will ask how often they have used AI for ten specific purposes (e.g., “For fun or entertainment”) on a five-point Likert scale (never, a few times a year, a few times a month, a few times a week, daily). However, only the second question (dummy coded) and two of the third question’s purposes relevant to learning (i.e., “To search for information or learn about something”; “To get advice on something”) will be used as measures of familiarity with the AI-podcast tools and previous AI use, respectively.", "One-way between-subjects design with five levels (control, misleading-article-only, misleading-podcast-only, misleading-podcast + passive inoculation, misleading-podcast + active inoculation), giving five total conditions that participants will be randomly assigned to using approximately equal cell sizes as the only constraint.", "To assess the effects of both misinformation and inoculation, we will perform one-way between-subjects ANOVAs with each dependent variable, using age or learning-relevant, previous-AI-use as covariates if significant correlations are found with them. Significant ANOVA results will be followed-up with hypothesis-based planned contrasts.", "To be included, participants on Prolific will have to have English fluency and have completed at least 10 previous studies with an overall approval rating of at least 98%. Datasets will be excluded if participants: indicate via an in-survey question that they were distracted while completing, or did not engage with, the experimental materials; demonstrate inadequate engagement with materials by answering every encoding question incorrectly; demonstrate, based on the 2.2 interquartile-range rule, either an upwardly outlying mean difference between normal and reverse-coded items or an upwardly outlying response SD for any question sets (indicative of erratic responding); or take longer than four hours to complete the study once opening it on Qualtrics. Further, participants familiar with NotebookLM were excluded in Experiment 1, as familiarity had a negative correlation with belief scores exclusively in the misleading-podcast-only condition; therefore, the same procedure will be implemented in this experiment if the same pattern repeats. If, however, an unexpectedly substantial number of participants are excluded, we will incrementally relax these criteria to regain experimental power without introducing significant bias.", "An a-priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) recommends a sample size of approximately 100 participants per experimental condition to detect a small difference between two between-subjects conditions (ƒ = .20, α = .05, 1 – β = .80). This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. #### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.
#### Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 21 distinct packages/libraries: BayesFactor, boot, broom, car, cowplot, dplyr, effectsize, emmeans, extrafont, ggplot2, haven, janitor, knitr, n, papaja, psych, readxl, sandwich, scales, stats, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.
#### Parsable code
All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

data_check.title: Data Check
data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 28 files: 6 data, 4 code, 5 documentation, 13 materials.
-  We found 6 tabular data files and extracted 1666 columns from 6 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2). We ran automated data-quality checks on 1666 columns; 28 columns have at least one potential issue (24 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 4 columns with inconsistent category casing; 4 columns with leading/trailing whitespace). 224 survey respondents were flagged for possible careless responding (26 of them only via short-scale straightlining, which can be normal answering). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender.

#### Careless Responding

224 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **26 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 file skipped as byte-identical duplicate of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  2 of 3 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  19 installable dependencies detected.
- 52 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 31 reported tests matched (0%).

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethics approval was obtained from the University of Western Australia Human Research Ethics Committee (RA/4/20/6423).
live_data_statements: Participants were randomly assigned to either listen to a misleading AI-generated podcast segment, read a misleading AI-generated article, or listen to a neutral nondeceptive AI-generated podcast segment, and they were told that the materials were AI-generated.
We recruited 501 Prolific (http://www.prolific.com/) users from the United States, who indicated English fluency and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.
Participants were randomly assigned to conditions, constrained only by approximately equal group sizes.
Participants were made aware of the article's AI source by two bold-font statements in the survey instructions stating ChatGPT to be the author.
That is, participants were asked to imagine themselves as an unscrupulous lobbyist paid to push some flawed position.
Participants first received an ethics-approved information page, provided informed consent via tick box, and indicated their age and gender.

An audio-check question was added to help ensure participants were able to listen to the podcast, and encoding questions were added to measure participants' engagement with materials (see Questionnaires below for details).
Prolific inclusion criteria were also identical except for the requirement that participants have at least 10 previously completed studies on the platform.
We recruited 550 Prolific users from the United States.
Participants were made aware of the article's AI source.

More specifically, like the original activity, participants were asked to imagine themselves as an unscrupulous lobbyist paid to push some flawed position; then they were asked to identify, for two flawed positions, which of three AI prompts would best produce biased information supporting each flawed position.

However, before choosing prompts in the new activity, participants were asked to choose: (i) which of three arguments they wanted to use (e.g., the health benefits of drinking lemon water), and (ii) which of two manipulation techniques they wanted to use (e.g., appeals to authority); this gave 18 (3 × 2 × 3) possible topic-technique-prompt configurations.

In addition to the questionnaires used in Experiment 1, we firstly added a multiplechoice audio-check question with ten response options that could only be answered if the participant had audio enabled (i.e., "Select the correct response [i.e., colour] given in the audio clip."); this helped to ensure that participants listened to the podcast.

However, another simple explanation could be that participants paid more attention to the article, as reading the article was quicker and less amenable to multitasking; this explanation may be unlikely though, since we excluded those with poor performance on encoding checks in Experiment 2.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("Experiment1_Analysis_Final.Rmd", 
"Experiment2_Analysis_Final.Rmd", "AI Podcast Rscript_Cleaned.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 2 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Experiment1_Analysis_Final.Rmd", "Experiment2_Analysis_Final.Rmd", 
"AI Podcast Rscript_Cleaned.R"), Outcome = c("ran_ok", "ran_ok", 
"errored"), Detail = c("", "", "undefined_variable"), "Time (s)" = c(23.2, 
23.8, 3)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "AI Podcast Rscript_Cleaned.R", "Missing variable" = "df1", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

2 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
*Expand a row below to see the output each script produced.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Output — Experiment1_Analysis_Final.Rmd (ran_ok)" collapse="true"}

> run_correlations <- function(data, vars, seed = STUDY$seed, R = STUDY$boot_R) {
> 
>   # Restricted to complete cases once, so the estimates, intervals and p-values
>   # all describe the same set of participants.
>   d_complete <- data[stats::complete.cases(data[, vars]), , drop = FALSE]
> 
>   set.seed(seed)
>   boot_result <- boot(
>     data = d_complete,
>     statistic = function(d, i) {
>       m <- cor(d[i, vars])
>       m[lower.tri(m)]
>     },
>     R = R)
> 
>   pair_indices <- which(lower.tri(cor(d_complete[, vars])), arr.ind = TRUE)
> 
>   # Variables are kept in separate columns so the pair label does not wrap.
>   results <- data.frame(
>     `Variable 1` = vars[pair_indices[, 1]],
>     `Variable 2` = vars[pair_indices[, 2]],
>     r = boot_result$t0, ci_lower = NA, ci_upper = NA,
>     check.names = FALSE)
> 
>   for (i in seq_len(nrow(pair_indices))) {
>     ci <- boot.ci(boot_result, type = "bca", index = i)
>     results$ci_lower[i] <- ci$bca[4]
>     results$ci_upper[i] <- ci$bca[5]
>   }
> 
>   results$p_value <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(pair_indices)), function(i) {
>     cor.test(d_complete[[vars[pair_indices[i, 1]]]],
>              d_complete[[vars[pair_indices[i, 2]]]])$p.value
>   })
> 
>   results %>%
>     mutate(`r [95% CI]` = paste0(printnum(r, digits = 2),
>                                  "\u00a0[", printnum(ci_lower, digits = 2), ",\u00a0",
>                                  printnum(ci_upper, digits = 2), "]"),
>            p = printp_nb(p_value)) %>%
>     select(`Variable 1`, `Variable 2`, `r [95% CI]`, p)
> }
> cor_apa <- run_correlations(df, cor_vars)

>                        seed = STUDY$seed, covariate_set = USE_COVARIATES) {
> 
>   dv_spec    <- DVS[[dv_key]]
>   covariates <- covs_for(dv_key, covariate_set)
> 
>   res   <- run_dv_analysis(dv_spec, data, contrast_list, covariates)
>   assum <- check_assumptions(res$model, data, dv_spec$var, covariates)
> 
>   # Welch's procedure cannot accommodate a covariate, so HC3 robust standard
>   # errors serve as its equivalent. Point estimates are unchanged by the choice

>   aov_robust      <- Anova(res$model, type = 3, white.adjust = "hc3")
>   emm_robust      <- emmeans(res$model, as.formula(paste("~", COND$var)),
>                              vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(res$model, type = "HC3"))
>   cons_robust_obj <- contrast(emm_robust, contrast_list)
>   cons_robust     <- summary(cons_robust_obj)
> 
>   # Which covariance matrix the reported tests and intervals come from.
>   levene_p <- assum$levene_raw[["Pr(>F)"]][1]
>   use_hc3 <- switch(STUDY$se_method,
>                     hc3    = TRUE,
>                     ols    = FALSE,
>                     levene = isTRUE(levene_p < STUDY$levene_alpha),
>                     both   = NA,
>                     stop("STUDY$se_method must be \"levene\", \"hc3\", ",

>   show <- if (is.na(use_hc3)) "both" else if (use_hc3) "hc3" else "ols"
>

>   } else {

> run_correlations <- function(data, vars, seed = STUDY$seed, R = STUDY$boot_R) {
> 
>   # Restricted to complete cases once, so the estimates, intervals and p-values
>   # all describe the same set of participants.
>   d_complete <- data[stats::complete.cases(data[, vars]), , drop = FALSE]
> 
>   set.seed(seed)
>   boot_result <- boot(
>     data = d_complete,
>     statistic = function(d, i) {
>       m <- cor(d[i, vars])
>       m[lower.tri(m)]
>     },
>     R = R)
> 
>   pair_indices <- which(lower.tri(cor(d_complete[, vars])), arr.ind = TRUE)
> 
>   # Variables are kept in separate columns so the pair label does not wrap.
>   results <- data.frame(
>     `Variable 1` = vars[pair_indices[, 1]],
>     `Variable 2` = vars[pair_indices[, 2]],
>     r = boot_result$t0, ci_lower = NA, ci_upper = NA,
>     check.names = FALSE)
> 
>   for (i in seq_len(nrow(pair_indices))) {
>     ci <- boot.ci(boot_result, type = "bca", index = i)
>     results$ci_lower[i] <- ci$bca[4]
>     results$ci_upper[i] <- ci$bca[5]
>   }
> 
>   results$p_value <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(pair_indices)), function(i) {
>     cor.test(d_complete[[vars[pair_indices[i, 1]]]],
>              d_complete[[vars[pair_indices[i, 2]]]])$p.value
>   })
> 
>   results %>%
>     mutate(`r [95% CI]` = paste0(printnum(r, digits = 2),
>                                  "\u00a0[", printnum(ci_lower, digits = 2), ",\u00a0",
>                                  printnum(ci_upper, digits = 2), "]"),
>            p = printp_nb(p_value)) %>%
>     select(`Variable 1`, `Variable 2`, `r [95% CI]`, p)
> }
> cor_apa <- run_correlations(df, cor_vars)

> build_rhs <- function(covariates) {
>   if (length(covariates) == 0) COND$var
>   else paste(COND$var, "+", paste(covariates, collapse = " + "))
> }
> boot_contrast_cis <- function(data, dv, rhs, emm_spec, contrast_list,
>                               R = STUDY$boot_R, seed = STUDY$seed) {
> 
>   n_con <- length(contrast_list)
>   form  <- as.formula(paste(dv, "~", rhs))
> 
>   stat_fun <- function(d, indices) {
>     out <- tryCatch({
>       mod <- lm(form, data = d[indices, ])
>       summary(contrast(emmeans(mod, emm_spec), contrast_list))$estimate
>     }, error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, n_con))
>     if (length(out) != n_con) rep(NA_real_, n_con) else out
>   }
> 
>   set.seed(seed)
>   bt <- boot(data = data, statistic = stat_fun, R = R)
> 
>   bounds <- t(vapply(seq_len(n_con), function(i) {
>     tryCatch(boot.ci(bt, type = "bca", index = i)$bca[4:5],
>              error = function(e) c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
>   }, numeric(2)))
> 
>   data.frame(contrast = names(contrast_list),
>              ci_lower = bounds[, 1], ci_upper = bounds[, 2],
>              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> }
> run_dv_analysis <- function(dv_spec, data, contrast_list, covariates) {
> 
>   dv  <- dv_spec$var
>   mod <- lm(as.formula(paste(dv, "~", build_rhs(covariates))), data = data)
> 
>   aov_obj   <- Anova(mod, type = 3)
>   emm       <- emmeans(mod, as.formula(paste("~", COND$var)))
>   cons      <- contrast(emm, contrast_list)
>   summ_cons <- summary(cons)
> 
>   # Plotted observations restricted to the model's listwise-deleted sample.
>   df_plot <- data %>%
>     filter(if_all(all_of(c(dv, COND$var, covariates)), ~ !is.na(.x)))
> 
>   # coord_cartesian() rather than scale_y_continuous(limits =), which would drop
>   # any bar or error bar falling outside the range.
>   p <- ggplot(as.data.frame(emm), aes(x = .data[[COND$var]], y = emmean,
>                                       fill = .data[[COND$var]])) +
>     geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.5) +
>     geom_jitter(data = df_plot, aes(x = .data[[COND$var]], y = .data[[dv]]),
>                 size = 0.5, position = position_jitter(width = 0.1)) +
>     scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = dv_spec$n_breaks)) +
>     coord_cartesian(ylim = dv_spec$y_coord) +
>     geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL), width = 0.2) +
>     scale_x_discrete(labels = COND$labels) +
>     xlab("Condition") + ylab(dv_spec$label) +
>     theme_bw() +
>     theme(legend.position = "none",
>           panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
>           panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
>           panel.border = element_blank(),
>           axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),
>           text = element_text(size = 24, family = "sans")) +
>     scale_fill_manual(values = COND$colours)
> 
>   list(model = mod, aov = aov_obj, eta_sq = eta_squared(aov_obj, partial = TRUE),
>        apa = apa_anova_table(aov_obj), fit = glance(mod),
>        emm = emm, emm_df = as.data.frame(emm), contrasts = cons,
>        contrasts_summary = summ_cons,
>        cohens_d = summ_cons$estimate / sigma(mod), plot = p)
> }
> check_assumptions <- function(model, data, dv, covariates) {
> 
>   levene_out <- leveneTest(as.formula(paste(dv, "~", COND$var)), data = data)
> 
>   # Homogeneity of regression slopes applies to ANCOVA only.
>   slopes_apa <- NULL
>   if (length(covariates) > 0) {
>     slopes_form <- as.formula(paste(dv, "~", COND$var, "*",
>                                     paste(covariates, collapse = " * ")))
>     slopes_apa <- apa_anova_table(Anova(lm(slopes_form, data = data), type = 3))
>   }
> 
>   list(levene = apa_levene_table(levene_out), levene_raw = levene_out,
>        slopes = slopes_apa)
> }
> assumption_plots <- function(model, label = "") {
>   op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
>   on.exit(par(op))
>   r <- residuals(model)
>   hist(r, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, main = paste("Residuals", label),
>        xlab = "Residual", col = "grey85", border = "white")
>   curve(dnorm(x, mean = mean(r), sd = sd(r)), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
>   qqnorm(r, main = paste("Q-Q Plot", label))
>   qqline(r, col = "red")
>   plot(fitted(model), r, main = paste("Residuals vs Fitted", label),
>        xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals", pch = 16,
>        col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3))
>   abline(h = 0, col = "red")
>   invisible(NULL)
> }
> analyse_dv <- function(dv_key, data, contrast_list,
>                        seed = STUDY$seed, covariate_set = USE_COVARIATES) {
> 
>   dv_spec    <- DVS[[dv_key]]
>   covariates <- covs_for(dv_key, covariate_set)
> 
>   res   <- run_dv_analysis(dv_spec, data, contrast_list, covariates)
>   assum <- check_assumptions(res$model, data, dv_spec$var, covariates)
> 
>   # Welch's procedure cannot accommodate a covariate, so HC3 robust standard
>   # errors serve as its equivalent. Point estimates are unchanged by the choice
>   # of covariance matrix; only the standard errors, tests and intervals differ.
>   aov_robust      <- Anova(res$model, type = 3, white.adjust = "hc3")
>   emm_robust      <- emmeans(res$model, as.formula(paste("~", COND$var)),
>                              vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(res$model, type = "HC3"))
>   cons_robust_obj <- contrast(emm_robust, contrast_list)
>   cons_robust     <- summary(cons_robust_obj)
> 
>   # Which covariance matrix the reported tests and intervals come from.
>   levene_p <- assum$levene_raw[["Pr(>F)"]][1]
>   use_hc3 <- switch(STUDY$se_method,
>                     hc3    = TRUE,
>                     ols    = FALSE,
>                     levene = isTRUE(levene_p < STUDY$levene_alpha),
>                     both   = NA,
>                     stop("STUDY$se_method must be \"levene\", \"hc3\", ",
>                          "\"ols\" or \"both\"."))
>   show <- if (is.na(use_hc3)) "both" else if (use_hc3) "hc3" else "ols"
> 
>   cis <- if (isTRUE(STUDY$boot_contrasts)) {
>     boot_contrast_cis(data = data, dv = dv_spec$var,
>                       rhs = build_rhs(covariates),
>                       emm_spec = as.formula(paste("~", COND$var)),
>                       contrast_list = contrast_list, seed = seed)
>   } else {
>     # The interval follows the same covariance matrix as the reported tests.
>     # Under "both" the conventional interval is shown, since it pairs with the
>     # first set of test columns.
>     src <- if (isTRUE(use_hc3)) cons_robust_obj else res$contrasts
>     ci  <- as.data.frame(confint(src))
>     data.frame(contrast = ci$contrast,
>                ci_lower = ci$lower.CL, ci_upper = ci$upper.CL,
>                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
>   }
> 
>   # d and its interval are the contrast estimate and interval divided by the
>   # residual standard deviation, so the interval tracks whichever covariance
>   # matrix produced cis above.
>   d_ci <- data.frame(lower = cis$ci_lower / sigma(res$model),
>                      upper = cis$ci_upper / sigma(res$model))
> 
>   tab <- merge_contrast_tests(res$contrasts_summary, cons_robust, cis,
>                               res$cohens_d, d_ci, show)
> 
>   list(results = res, assumptions = assum, cis = cis, aov_robust = aov_robust,
>        contrasts_robust = cons_robust, covariates = covariates, table = tab,
>        use_hc3 = use_hc3, show = show, levene_p = levene_p,
>        # The robust omnibus table is redundant when only conventional tests are
>        # reported, so the chunks that print it are gated on this.
>        show_robust = !identical(show, "ols"))
> }

text.text: We have no known conflict of interest to disclose.
Generative artificial-intelligence (AI) tools continue to grow in popularity.
However, AI tools can be biased, erroneous, and used to nefariously create misleading content.
Consequently, newer AI tools that generate realistic audio could be concerning, as people increasingly consume audiovisual news and educational media (e.g., podcasts).
The present study investigated whether a misleading AI-generated podcast impacted relevant beliefs and could be counteracted through a pre-emptive technique called inoculation.

Inoculation interventions warn people about a deceptive persuasive attack, then prepare them by providing relevant counterarguments, explaining deceptive persuasion techniques, or discrediting likely misinformation sources.
Such inoculation interventions can provide information passively or actively engage recipients via educational activities, with the latter approach considered superior.
While inoculation has demonstrated effectiveness against textual misinformation, it has not been tested against misleading AI-generated audio.

Therefore, across two experiments, we investigated: (1) how an AI-generated podcast (vs. written article) falsely claiming that sunscreen nanoparticles are a health hazard (Experiment 1) or that microwaves deplete food nutrition (Experiment 2) influenced beliefs, and general trust in AI-generated information; and (2) if an active (vs. passive) AI-source-focused inoculation reduced these belief and trust effects.
Participants either received a misleading article, a misleading podcast, or a nondeceptive podcast (control condition).

The misleading podcast was preceded either by: a passive inoculation explaining how AI-generated information can be used to mislead, an active inoculation that added an educational activity demonstrating deceptive techniques, or no intervention.
Results showed that the podcast and article produced comparable increases in false-claim belief.
Both inoculations reduced misinformed beliefs while not eliminating the misinformation's effect, and significantly reduced general trust in AI-generated information.
These findings show that AI-generated audio can influence health-related beliefs as strongly as textual misinformation, and that a brief AI-source-focused inoculation mitigated its persuasive impact.
This research informs interventions targeting emerging forms of AI-driven misinformation.
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) continues to proliferate.
In particular, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT draw over 2 billion monthly visits (Liu & Wang, 2026), mainly for information-seeking purposes (Chatterji et al., 2025).

text.text: As LLMs continue to suffer from issues like biased training data and information fabrication (Chelli et al., 2024; Nygren et al., 2025; Saeidnia et al., 2026), concerns remain over the potential for AI tools to exacerbate both unintentional and nefarious misinformation spread (Schlicht, 2025; Shukla & Tripathi, 2024; A. Williams et al., 2025)</ref>; for the latter, AI has substantially lowered the resources (e.g., time, skill, capital) required to produce and disseminate misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Goldstein et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Nyhan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, AI-generated misinformation can be as persuasive as human-authored equivalents (Spitale et al., 2023), hence the principal risk may lay in the scale, speed, and accessibility of misleading-AI content.

text.text: All of these factors may worsen the detrimental impacts of misinformation on individuals and society (de Ridder, 2024; Ecker et al., 2024; Lewandowsky, 2024).

text.text: One potential avenue for AI-generated misinformation to influence audiences is through realistic but synthetic audio content such as podcasts, which could be particularly engaging (e.g., Li & Ensafjoo, 2025; Mayer, 2005).

text.text: Contemporary information consumption is increasingly shifting towards audio and video modalities.
Podcasts in particular-including news and health-related podcasts-have grown in popularity (Newman, 2025; Shearer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Podcasts in particular-including news and health-related podcasts-have grown in popularity <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Newman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Shearer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While many podcasts serve an educational function, podcast consumers tend to report entertainment as a primary motivation to listen (Chan-Olmsted & Wang, 2022; Chou et al., 2023; Craig et al., 2023; Whittle, 2024).
text.formatted: While many podcasts serve an educational function, podcast consumers tend to report entertainment as a primary motivation to listen <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chan-Olmsted & Wang, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Chou et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Craig et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Whittle, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This engagement comes partly from podcast characteristics such as storytelling to build suspense and a conversational tone that can induce emotional connection between host and listener (Lindgren, 2022 (Lindgren, , 2023;; Nee & Santana, 2022).
text.formatted: This engagement comes partly from podcast characteristics such as storytelling to build suspense and a conversational tone that can induce emotional connection between host and listener <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lindgren, 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lindgren, , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Nee & Santana, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such narrative techniques have been shown to promote attitudinal changes via both visual and auditory modalities (Braddock & Dillard, 2016; Shen et al., 2015), reduce counterargumentation (M. C. Green & Brock, 2000), and increase persuasion by masking persuasive intent (Crano et al., 2007; Walster & Festinger, 1962); these techniques may also be more effective in audio versus text format (Braverman, 2008; Riggs & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2024).

C. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Green & Brock, 2000)</ref>, and increase persuasion by masking persuasive intent <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Crano et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Walster & Festinger, 1962)</ref>; these techniques may also be more effective in audio versus text format <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Braverman, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Riggs & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, podcasts have been found to directly induce counter-attitudinal shifts (Kurdi et al., 2022) and may present a real risk for misinformation spread (Caramancion, 2022).

text.text: Moreover, in contrast to written articles, synthetic podcasts add the deceptive layer of fabricating the speakers; a podcast could thus be perceived as a genuine human exchange that produced a consensus (Mai et al., 2023; Weaver et al., 2007), when in fact a single AI system was the source.

text.text: Despite concerns about the ability of AI tools to produce realistic podcast content, the small number of extant studies investigating cognitive impacts of AI-generated misinformation has focused solely on written text (Hwang & Jeong, 2025; Lee & Liu, 2025; McIlhiney et al., 2026; Shin et al., 2025; Spearing et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Despite concerns about the ability of AI tools to produce realistic podcast content, the small number of extant studies investigating cognitive impacts of AI-generated misinformation has focused solely on written text <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hwang & Jeong, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lee & Liu, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Shin et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Spearing et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: No research, to our knowledge, has directly tested the cognitive impacts of a misleading AI-generated podcast and the efficacy of countermeasures; the present study sought to address this gap in the literature.

It is well-documented that while debunking false claims retrospectively is beneficial, misinformation often continues to impact people's thinking even after clear and direct corrections (i.e., the continued influence effect; Ecker et al., 2022; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020).
text.formatted: It is well-documented that while debunking false claims retrospectively is beneficial, misinformation often continues to impact people's thinking even after clear and direct corrections (i.e., the continued influence effect; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Ecker et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, researchers have increasingly explored ways of pre-emptively protecting people from misinformation effects (Kozyreva et al., 2024; Lewandowsky & van der Linden, 2021).
text.formatted: Consequently, researchers have increasingly explored ways of pre-emptively protecting people from misinformation effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kozyreva et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Lewandowsky & van der Linden, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Based on inoculation theory (McGuire, 1964), such techniques initially alert people to a potentially impending deception to foster a counter-argumentative stance, before prebunking an anticipated misleading argument or explaining a persuasive technique that is often used to mislead (Cook et al., 2017; Maertens et al., 2020; Roozenbeek et al., 2022; M. N. Williams & Bond, 2020).
text.formatted: Based on inoculation theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(McGuire, 1964)</ref>, such techniques initially alert people to a potentially impending deception to foster a counter-argumentative stance, before prebunking an anticipated misleading argument or explaining a persuasive technique that is often used to mislead <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cook et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Maertens et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Roozenbeek et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">M. N. Williams & Bond, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A few recent studies have also explored sourcefocused inoculations, which rely on discreditation of a likely source of future misinformation (Ecker et al., 2024; McIlhiney et al., 2026; Spearing et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A few recent studies have also explored sourcefocused inoculations, which rely on discreditation of a likely source of future misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ecker et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Spearing et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While inoculation strategies are often passive and merely present information to recipients, they can also include active components that encourage recipients to consider possible persuasive arguments or techniques, self-generate potential counterarguments, or engage with educational materials in an interactive way (i.e., active inoculation).

Both passive inoculation (Cook et al., 2017; Maertens et al., 2020; McIlhiney et al., 2026; Tay et al., 2022; van der Linden et al., 2017; Williams & Bond, 2020) and active inoculation (M. Green et al., 2022; McIlhiney et al., 2026; Roozenbeek et al., 2022; Roozenbeek & van der Linden, 2019a , 2019b) have been found to reduce misinformation belief and sharing, and improve truth discernment.
text.formatted: Both passive inoculation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cook et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Maertens et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tay et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">van der Linden et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Williams & Bond, 2020)</ref> and active inoculation (M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Green et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Roozenbeek et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Roozenbeek & van der Linden, 2019a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">, 2019b)</ref> have been found to reduce misinformation belief and sharing, and improve truth discernment.

text.text: There is some evidence, however, that active inoculation may be more effective at combatting both human misinformation (M. Green et al., 2022) and AI-generated misinformation (McIlhiney et al., 2026), which is argued to be partly due to greater cognitive engagement in the active component (McGuire & Papageorgis, 1961; Tyler et al., 1979). Green et al. (2022) found that only active inoculation reduced the perceived persuasiveness and reliability of a misleading article about extreme weather events, although this effect was nonsignificant when accounting for covariates related to worldview and climate-change beliefs.

(2022)</ref> found that only active inoculation reduced the perceived persuasiveness and reliability of a misleading article about extreme weather events, although this effect was nonsignificant when accounting for covariates related to worldview and climate-change beliefs.

text.text: Meanwhile, McIlhiney et al. (2026) presented participants with an AI-generated article about the alleged dangers of nanoparticles in sunscreen, preceded either by a passive AI-source-focused inoculation, an active AIsource-focused inoculation, or no intervention.
text.formatted: Meanwhile, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al. (2026)</ref> presented participants with an AI-generated article about the alleged dangers of nanoparticles in sunscreen, preceded either by a passive AI-source-focused inoculation, an active AIsource-focused inoculation, or no intervention.

text.text: The passive inoculation explained how AIgenerated information can be misleading and maliciously misused; the active inoculation additionally engaged participants in an educational activity that required them to identify AI prompts best suited to producing misleading information.
Results showed that both passive and active inoculation reduced general trust in AI-generated information and specific misinformation-related beliefs, with active inoculation having larger effects.
Therefore, current evidence suggests that active inoculation could outperform passive inoculation at building resistance to misinformation from human and AI sources.

Experiment 1 aimed to investigate the effect of a misleading AI-generated audio podcast (vs. written article) on claim belief, and the effectiveness of an active (vs. passive) AI-source-focused inoculation to (1) reduce general trust in AI-generated information, and (2) reduce the influence of the specific misinformation provided on relevant beliefs.

Participants were randomly assigned to either listen to a misleading AI-generated podcast segment, read a misleading AI-generated article, or listen to a neutral nondeceptive AI-generated podcast segment, and they were told that the materials were AI-generated.
The topic of both the misleading podcast and article was the alleged dangers of nanoparticles in sunscreen, following McIlhiney et al. (2026).
text.formatted: The topic of both the misleading podcast and article was the alleged dangers of nanoparticles in sunscreen, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: Participants who listened to the misleading podcast either received: a pre-emptive passive inoculation discrediting generative AI sources by explaining how their outputs can mislead, supplemented by a demonstrative example; an active inoculation providing the same explanation and example but alongside an interactive educational activity; or no intervention.
Note that while AI naturally relies on human input, we treat it as the primary misinformation source.
Questionnaires were used to measure general trust in AI-generated information and specific beliefs regarding nanoparticles in sunscreen; previous AI usage was also measured.
We firstly hypothesised that both passive inoculation (H1a) and active inoculation (H1b) would reduce general trust in AI information, with a stronger effect for active inoculation (H2).
We further hypothesised that AI-generated misinformation in written format (H3a) and audio-podcast format (H3b) would influence beliefs, with a stronger effect for the audio format (H4).
Third, we predicted that the impact of the podcast would be reduced by passive inoculation (H5a) and active inoculation (H5b), with a stronger effect for active inoculation (H6).
However, we hypothesised that the effects of misinformation on belief would persist after both passive (H7a) and active inoculation (H7b); that is, we predicted a continued influence effect.

The experiment used a between-subjects design with five conditions: control (nondeceptive podcast); AI podcast (misleading AI podcast); AI article (misleading AI article); passive inoculation + AI podcast (AI-source-focused inoculation followed by misleading AI podcast); and active inoculation + AI podcast (AI-source-focused inoculation with educational activity followed by misleading AI podcast).
The two dependent variables were general trust in AI-generated information, and misinformation-congruent beliefs.

Age and previous AI usage were included as potential covariates, based on previous work showing a correlation between these variables and the dependent variables (McIlhiney et al., 2025 (McIlhiney et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Age and previous AI usage were included as potential covariates, based on previous work showing a correlation between these variables and the dependent variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(McIlhiney et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McIlhiney et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Ethics approval was obtained from the University of Western Australia Human Research Ethics Committee (RA/4/20/6423).
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.

Using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007), an a priori power analysis suggested a sample size of 100 participants per experimental condition to detect a small difference between two conditions (f = 0.2, α = .05, and 1 -β = .80).

text.text: We recruited 501 Prolific (http://www.prolific.com/) users from the United States, who indicated English fluency and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.
text.formatted: We recruited 501 Prolific (<ref type="url" target="http://www.prolific.com/">www.prolific.com</ref>) users from the United States, who indicated English fluency and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions, constrained only by approximately equal group sizes.
Average age was M = 46.44 years (SD = 13.60, range 20-83), with 218 men, 276 women, and 6 non-binary participants.

Participants' data were excluded if they: indicated inadequate effort (see Materials; n = 1); demonstrated an upwardly outlying (following the 2.2 interquartile-range rule) mean difference score between normal and reverse-coded belief questions (indicating uniform responding; n = 28) or an upwardly outlying response SD for belief and trust questions (indicative of erratic responding; n = 0); or had a completion time longer than four hours (n = 0).
These exclusions left a final sample size of N = 472.
Participants in the AI-article condition were given a 503-word article generated with the free version of ChatGPT-4o, titled "The Hidden Danger: Is Nanotechnology in Sunscreen Harming Your Health?"
(adapted from McIlhiney et al., 2026).
text.formatted: (adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The article provided a biased account of the dangers of nanoparticles in sunscreen (e.g., "sunscreen has been promoted as an essential safeguard against skin cancer […but…] a growing body of research now raises troubling questions about the invisible additives lurking in these products-namely, nanoparticles […which…] may be doing more harm than good") supported by fictional expert statements (e.g., "Dr.

Emilia Vargas, a nanotoxicologist at the Lorne Institute of Biomedical Research, warns that 'the assumption that nanoparticles like titanium dioxide (TiO₂) and zinc oxide (ZnO) remain on the skin's surface is scientifically naive.'").
Participants were made aware of the article's AI source by two bold-font statements in the survey instructions stating ChatGPT to be the author.

The free version of NotebookLM (based on Gemini 2.5 Flash) was used to generate a 387 s audio-podcast segment based on the misleading AI-generated article about nanoparticles in sunscreen (outlined above).

More specifically, the article's content was converted into an engaging conversation between two (male and female) podcast hosts; this conversation was framed as a deep dive into the central topic, intended to teach listeners and raise awareness.
An excerpt is produced below (the full script is available in the Online Supplement).
As shown in the preceding example, the realism of the conversation was enhanced by affirming interjections and vocal disfluencies, as well as the natural rhythm of speech due to breathing.
We further enhanced the perceived authenticity of the podcast by adding royaltyfree intro and outro music.

Participants in the control condition were given a neutral 285 s AI-generated podcast about the retirement of a fictional radio host generated in NotebookLM using an article titled "A Decade of Voices: Reflecting on a Local Radio Legend's Journey" (adapted from Spearing et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Participants in the control condition were given a neutral 285 s AI-generated podcast about the retirement of a fictional radio host generated in NotebookLM using an article titled "A Decade of Voices: Reflecting on a Local Radio Legend's Journey" (adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Spearing et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The article broadly covered the host's career (e.g., "Local talk-back radio presenter Jim Morgan is signing off after a decade of being the voice that stirred mornings and sparked debates in our community.").

To preserve some relevance with the questionnaires, the article referenced the host's regular discussions of science topics, and shared an example science tidbit (i.e., Morgan quoted saying "Did you know that there are more possible games of chess than there are stars in the universe?
I didn't until a caller shared it in a discussion last week.").

Participants in the passive-inoculation + AI podcast condition were given a 228-word article titled "The Limitations of AI Technology" (adapted from Spearing et al., 2025), highlighting how AI can be used, maliciously or unintentionally, to produce inaccurate or biased information.
text.formatted: Participants in the passive-inoculation + AI podcast condition were given a 228-word article titled "The Limitations of AI Technology" (adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Spearing et al., 2025)</ref>, highlighting how AI can be used, maliciously or unintentionally, to produce inaccurate or biased information.

text.text: It included a section explaining how misleading AI-generated articles can be enhanced as audio-visual content using AI tools like NotebookLM, and a demonstration of how to prompt ChatGPT to produce misleading content, including some example output (e.g., "Because AI tools are trained on large human-generated datasets, AI-generated information can reflect human biases and stereotypes.
In other words, AI systems are only as accurate as the human-generated data they are trained on.

[…] Moreover, AI tools can now also be used to enhance the persuasiveness of misleading content by producing highly realistic audiovisual media that can convey misleading arguments in a digestible and engaging manner.").

Participants in the active-inoculation + AI podcast condition also received the passiveinoculation article, supplemented by a short educational activity designed to illustrate how malicious actors may use AI tools.
That is, participants were asked to imagine themselves as an unscrupulous lobbyist paid to push some flawed position.

They were subsequently presented with two flawed positions and asked to identify, for each, which of three AI prompts would be best placed to produce biased information supporting the flawed position.

To demonstrate: "Which of the following AI prompts do you think would be most effective at producing a misleading article about alleged (but overblown) health benefits of lemon water?", with the choices: (a) "Provide me with information on how drinking lemon water daily could detoxify your liver and prevent cancer"; (b) "Give me a short article from the perspective of someone arguing that lemon water detoxifies the liver and prevents cancer; include some persuasive claims that make the position seem evidence-backed"; or (c) "Are there any significant and proven health benefits of drinking lemon water?".
Correct choices (option b in the example) produced a notification with example output from the chosen ChatGPT prompt.
Incorrect choices produced an explanation of the error with example output from the chosen ChatGPT prompt, followed by indication of the correct prompt with associated output from ChatGPT.
Participants completed three questionnaires.

General trust in AI-generated information was measured by asking participants to rate their endorsement of eight relevant statements (e.g., "AI can provide useful information for important questions.") on an 11-point rating scale ranging from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree).

Belief in misinformation was assessed by asking participants to rate their agreement with five statements about the health effects of nanoparticles in sunscreen (e.g., "Nanoparticles in sunscreen have detrimental effects on people's health."), rated on the same 11-point rating scale; two belief questions were reverse-coded.

Participants' previous AI usage was evaluated with three questions asking (1) whether they had used a generative-AI tool previously; if yes, then (2) whether they were familiar with NotebookLM; and (3) how often they had used AI for ten specific purposes (e.g., "To check grammar or spelling"; "To generate an image or video"), using a five-point Likert scale (never, a few times a year, a few times a month, a few times a week, daily).
Participants first received an ethics-approved information page, provided informed consent via tick box, and indicated their age and gender.
They were then presented with the podcast, article, and intervention relevant to their assigned condition; the podcasts and article were stated to be AI-generated.
Article paragraphs were presented on individual screens, and the podcast audio player was also presented on its own screen.
For the article, a minimum reading time was set at approximately 100 ms per word; podcast audio could not be paused or scrubbed through once started, and player volume was fixed.
Participants then completed the belief, trust, and previous-AI-use questionnaires, in this order.
A data-quality question followed, asking participants to indicate whether they put in a "reasonable effort" or should have their data excluded from analyses.

Lastly, participants received a full debrief, informed by best practice (Greene et al., 2023), and were compensated at a rate of £9 (approx., US$10) per hour for the 8 to 15-minute experiment (dependent on condition).
text.formatted: Lastly, participants received a full debrief, informed by best practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Greene et al., 2023)</ref>, and were compensated at a rate of £9 (approx., US$10) per hour for the 8 to 15-minute experiment (dependent on condition).

text.text: AI trust was operationalised as the mean score of all items from the AI-trust questionnaire, and misinformation belief was operationalised as the mean score from the belief questionnaire; scores ranged from 0 to 10, where higher scores indicated higher trust and stronger misinformation belief, respectively.
AI use was operationalised as the mean of the two AI-use-questionnaire items relevant to learning.
Previous experience with NotebookLM was coded as a binary variable (No = 0, Yes = 1).

As we previously found that trust in AI-generated information (hereon AI trust) correlated with age and previous AI use (hereon AI use), and beliefs in AI-generated misinformation (hereon misinformation beliefs) correlated with AI use (see McIlhiney et al., 2026), a correlation analysis was firstly performed with these variables.
text.formatted: As we previously found that trust in AI-generated information (hereon AI trust) correlated with age and previous AI use (hereon AI use), and beliefs in AI-generated misinformation (hereon misinformation beliefs) correlated with AI use (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026)</ref>, a correlation analysis was firstly performed with these variables.

text.text: As shown in Table 1, AI trust had positive correlations with age (small), AI use (large), and NotebookLM experience (small), suggesting that older age and greater previous AI use were associated with higher trust in AI-generated information.
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, AI trust had positive correlations with age (small), AI use (large), and NotebookLM experience (small), suggesting that older age and greater previous AI use were associated with higher trust in AI-generated information.

text.text: Meanwhile, misinformation belief had a positive correlation with AI use (small) but a negative correlation with NotebookLM experience (small); thus, while greater previous AI use was associated with stronger belief in AI-generated misinformation, the opposite was true for previous NotebookLM use.

Further analysis showed that the correlation between misinformation belief and NotebookLM experience was only significant in the AI-podcast condition (see online supplement); as this violates the homogeneity-of-slopes assumption for ANCOVA, we excluded participants in the podcast condition indicating previous NotebookLM experience (n = 9 after other exclusions).

To foreshadow, the abovementioned exclusions and covariate inclusion produced stronger inoculation effects on AI trust and misinformation beliefs when compared to supplemental analyses using the full sample and no covariates (see online supplement).

For AI trust, this was mainly due to reduced error variance across conditions after accounting for the (large) effect of previous AI use; for misinformation belief, it was mainly due to an increased estimate in the podcast condition after excluding those with previous NotebookLM experience.
First, the effectiveness of inoculation to reduce AI trust was tested.
A one-way ANCOVA on mean AI-trust scores with age and AI use as covariates returned a significant main effect of condition, F(4, 456) = 10.76, p < .001, η² = .09 (see Figure 1).

text.text: These showed lower trust in AI-generated information in the inoculation + AI-podcast conditions than the AI-podcast condition, confirming our predictions that passive and active inoculation would effectively reduce trust.

However, note that in the supplemental analysis with no covariates and the full sample, the effects of both inoculations were smaller, with active inoculation's effect becoming nonsignificant (see online supplement).
We also found no support for H2, as there were no significant differences in AI trust between passive-and active-inoculation + AIpodcast conditions.

Further, both inoculation conditions demonstrated significantly lower belief scores than the AI-podcast condition, demonstrating efficacy for both passive (H5a) and active (H5b) inoculation against audio-podcast misinformation.

However, note that the results of the supplemental analysis with no covariates and the full sample showed the effect of passive inoculation to be non-significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction (see Online Supplement).

Experiment 1 examined the influence of a misleading AI-generated audio podcast (vs.

written article) on relevant beliefs, and how effectively passive and active AI-source-focused inoculations reduce general trust in AI-generated information and specific misinformation influence on beliefs.

Misinformation influenced beliefs when it was presented either in written or podcast format; however, the prediction that the podcast would have a stronger effect on beliefs than the article was rejected, with a numerically larger effect for the article.

Both inoculations reduced general trust in AI-generated information and endorsement of specific misinformation-relevant claims; however, when not accounting for the covariate effects of previous AI use and age, only passive inoculation was significantly effective for AI trust and only active inoculation was significantly effective for beliefs (after Holm-Bonferroni correction).
Passive and active inoculation were not found to be significantly different for both outcomes, rejecting the predicted superiority of active inoculation.

Neither intervention completely eliminated misinformation's influence on belief, replicating previous findings of continued misinformation influence across various contexts and measures (Ecker et al., 2022).

text.text: Given that (i) only one misleading topic was used, (ii) findings were inconsistent between models with and without covariates, and (iii) active-inoculation findings contradicted the bulk of previous evidence, we decided to run a pre-registered (https://osf.io/czax3) follow-up experiment for robustness.
text.formatted: Given that (i) only one misleading topic was used, (ii) findings were inconsistent between models with and without covariates, and (iii) active-inoculation findings contradicted the bulk of previous evidence, we decided to run a pre-registered (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/czax3">https://osf.io/czax3</ref>) follow-up experiment for robustness.

text.text: Experiment 2 again aimed to investigate the effects of a misleading AI-generated audio podcast (vs. written article) and AI-source-focused inoculation on trust in AI-generated information and relevant beliefs.

Participants again engaged with either a misleading AIgenerated podcast segment, misleading AI-generated article, or a neutral nondeceptive AIgenerated podcast segment, which they knew were AI-generated.
The new topic of the misleading podcast and article was the false claim that microwaves degrade the nutritional value of food.
As before, participants who listened to the misleading AI podcast received either a passive inoculation, active inoculation, or no intervention.

However, we attempted to further distinguish the active from the passive inoculation by making the active component more engaging; we also shortened the active inoculation to more closely match the length of the passive inoculation (see Materials section for further details).

Questionnaires were again used to measure general trust in AI-generated information, specific misinformation-relevant beliefs (i.e., beliefs regarding negative impacts of microwaves on food nutrition), and previous AI usage.
Hypotheses were identical to Experiment 1.
Experiment 2 used the same one-way between-subjects design and variables as Experiment 1.

An audio-check question was added to help ensure participants were able to listen to the podcast, and encoding questions were added to measure participants' engagement with materials (see Questionnaires below for details).
All materials and data can be found online at: https://osf.io/nwt8a.
text.formatted: All materials and data can be found online at: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/nwt8a">https://osf.io/nwt8a</ref>.

text.text: Power calculations and condition randomisation were identical to Experiment 1.
Prolific inclusion criteria were also identical except for the requirement that participants have at least 10 previously completed studies on the platform.
We recruited 550 Prolific users from the United States.
Average age was M = 41.56 years (SD = 13.65, range 18-82), with 206 men, 333 women, 10 non-binary participants, and 1 participant who preferred to self-describe their gender.

Participants' data were excluded if they: indicated that they thought their effort was inadequate (see Materials; n = 8); failed to answer at least one of three encoding-check questions correctly (see Materials; n = 30); demonstrated an upwardly outlying (following the 2.2 interquartile-range rule) mean difference between normal and reverse-coded trust and belief questions (indicating uniform responding; n = 9) or an upwardly outlying response SD for trust and belief questions (indicative of erratic responding; n = 2); or had a completion time longer than four hours (n = 1).
These exclusions left a final sample size of N = 500.
Participants in the AI-article condition were given a 530-word article generated with the free version of ChatGPT-4o, titled "Microwaves: The Hidden Threat to Your Food's Nutritional Value".

The article provided a misleading account of how microwaves deleteriously impact food nutrition (e.g., "For decades, microwave ovens have been celebrated for their speed and convenience […but…] recent claims from independent researchers suggest that the technology may be silently undermining the nutritional integrity of our food […which…] could degrade essential nutrients in ways traditional cooking methods do not").
These claims were supported by fictional expert statements (e.g., "Dr.

Harriet Sloan, a nutrition biochemist at the Northbridge Institute of Dietary Research, asserts that 'microwaves expose food molecules to rapid, high-frequency oscillations that can disrupt the chemical bonds in vitamins and antioxidants, rendering them inactive.'").
Participants were made aware of the article's AI source.

The free version of NotebookLM (based on Gemini 3.5) was used to generate a 352 s audio-podcast segment based on the misleading AI-generated article about microwaves damaging food nutrition (outlined above).
An excerpt is produced below.
The control podcast was identical to that used in Experiment 1.
The passive inoculation was identical to that used in Experiment 1, except for updates to the demonstrative example.

More specifically, we created five additional versions of the demonstrative example, for a total of six; these six versions matched all possible configurations that resulted from participants' choices in the active-inoculation educational activity (see next section for full details).
Each participant in the passive-inoculation condition saw one of these demonstrative-example versions, which were randomly assigned using approximately equal sample sizes as the only constraint.

Further, AI podcast snippets for the updated demonstrative example were (re-)generated using the AI media-editing suite Wondercraft (http://www.wondercraft.ai/ Gemini-TTS model); this was done so that inoculation podcast snippets used different voices to the main podcast segments.
text.formatted: Further, AI podcast snippets for the updated demonstrative example were (re-)generated using the AI media-editing suite Wondercraft (<ref type="url" target="http://www.wondercraft.ai/">www.wondercraft.ai;</ref> Gemini-TTS model); this was done so that inoculation podcast snippets used different voices to the main podcast segments.

text.text: The active inoculation received two changes from Experiment 1.

First, we merged the demonstrative example with the educational activity; this both shortened the active inoculation to be closer in length to the passive inoculation and formed part of our modifications to make the active component more engaging.
Second, the active component (i.e., educational activity) was expanded.

More specifically, like the original activity, participants were asked to imagine themselves as an unscrupulous lobbyist paid to push some flawed position; then they were asked to identify, for two flawed positions, which of three AI prompts would best produce biased information supporting each flawed position.

However, before choosing prompts in the new activity, participants were asked to choose: (i) which of three arguments they wanted to use (e.g., the health benefits of drinking lemon water), and (ii) which of two manipulation techniques they wanted to use (e.g., appeals to authority); this gave 18 (3 × 2 × 3) possible topic-technique-prompt configurations.
The full inoculation materials are in the Online Supplement.

In addition to the questionnaires used in Experiment 1, we firstly added a multiplechoice audio-check question with ten response options that could only be answered if the participant had audio enabled (i.e., "Select the correct response [i.e., colour] given in the audio clip."); this helped to ensure that participants listened to the podcast.

Further, three multiple-choice questions were used to check encoding of the information provided in the misleading article/podcast, which provided four options (e.g., "Which cooking method was not mentioned?"
Roasting, b.
Slow-cooking, c.
Steaming, d.
Sautéing).
Finally, we updated the NotebookLM familiarity question to also mention Wondercraft, as we now used the latter to generate the inoculation podcast-snippets.

The audio-check question was given at the beginning of the experiment (after the demographics questions and before condition assignment), while the encoding questions were given after presentation of the article/podcast, just before the belief questions.
The procedure was otherwise identical to Experiment 1.

As shown in Table 4, AI trust had positive correlations with age (medium), AI use (large), and NotebookLM-Wondercraft experience (medium), suggesting, as in Experiment 1, that older age and greater previous AI use were associated with higher trust in AI-generated information.
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>, AI trust had positive correlations with age (medium), AI use (large), and NotebookLM-Wondercraft experience (medium), suggesting, as in Experiment 1, that older age and greater previous AI use were associated with higher trust in AI-generated information.

text.text: However, while misinformation belief had a positive correlation with AI use (small) as in Experiment 1, no significant correlation was found with NotebookLM-Wondercraft experience, including in the AI-podcast condition; thus, only greater general AI experience was associated with stronger belief in AI-generated misinformation.
The significant correlates were included as covariates in the relevant models.
We first tested the effectiveness of inoculation to reduce AI trust.
A one-way ANCOVA on mean AI-trust scores with age and AI use as covariates returned a significant main effect of condition, F(4, 493) = 7.25, p < .001, η² = .06 (see Figure 3).

text.text: Like Experiment 1, these showed lower trust in AI-generated information in the passive-and active-inoculation + podcast conditions than the AI-podcast condition, confirming our predictions that passive and active inoculation would effectively reduce trust.
Unlike Experiment 1, these results were consistent in a supplemental analysis with no covariates and the full sample.
There was again no significant differences in AI trust between passive-and active-inoculation + podcast conditions, rejecting H2.
A significant Levene's test again suggested the White adjustment for heteroskedasticity.

A one-way ANCOVA on mean belief scores with AI use as a covariate yielded a significant main effect of condition, F(4, 494) = 32.88, p < .001, η² = .17 (see Figure 4), with the AI-use covariate also significant, F(1, 494) = 11.63, p < .001, η² = .03.
