text.text: More specifically, both the AIarticle and AI-podcast conditions showed higher misinformation-congruent belief scores than the control condition, showing that AI-generated written (H3a) and audio-podcast (H3b) misinformation influenced belief.

H4 was not supported, as no significant difference was found between AI-article and AI-podcast conditions; though, unlike Experiment 1, the podcast condition was associated with a numerically greater effect on belief.

Further, both inoculation + AI-podcast conditions demonstrated significantly lower belief scores than the AI-podcast condition, demonstrating efficacy for both passive (H5a) and active (H5b) inoculation against audio-podcast misinformation; unlike Experiment 1, these results were consistent with the supplemental analysis using no covariates and the full sample (see online supplement).
In line with Experiment 1, no significant difference was found between the inoculation conditions, rejecting H6.

Finally, belief scores in the control condition were lower than in both inoculation + AI-podcast conditions, meaning neither intervention eliminated the podcast's effect on beliefs (i.e., a continued influence effect; supporting H7a and H7b).

Experiment 2 largely replicated the findings of Experiment 1 using different materials and an enhanced active inoculation, demonstrating more-consistent effects overall.

Misinformation influenced beliefs when it was presented either in written or podcast format; while the effect of the podcast was numerically larger, the difference was nonsignificant, again rejecting the hypothesis of a stronger podcast effect.

Both inoculations reduced general trust in AI-generated information and endorsement of specific misinformation-relevant claims, with passive and active inoculation demonstrating no difference, rejecting the predicted superiority of active inoculation; in fact, passive inoculation's effect was numerically larger.
However, neither intervention completely eliminated misinformation's influence on belief, replicating Experiment 1's continued influence effect.
This study demonstrated a clear effect of AI-generated podcast misinformation on relevant health beliefs.
In contrast to predictions, however, misinformation had a similar effect on beliefs regardless of format (article vs. podcast) across two experiments.
This finding may indicate that the format of misleading information is relatively inconsequential.

However, another simple explanation could be that participants paid more attention to the article, as reading the article was quicker and less amenable to multitasking; this explanation may be unlikely though, since we excluded those with poor performance on encoding checks in Experiment 2.

Alternatively, the finding could relate to Chaiken and Eagly's (1976) observation that persuasion regarding complex topics may be more effective in a written versus audio format, with audio persuasion more susceptible to effects of communicator likeability (Chaiken & Eagly, 1983).
text.formatted: Alternatively, the finding could relate to <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Chaiken and Eagly's (1976)</ref> observation that persuasion regarding complex topics may be more effective in a written versus audio format, with audio persuasion more susceptible to effects of communicator likeability <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Chaiken & Eagly, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, if participants in the current study found the topic complex or the podcast hosts unlikable, this may have lessened the impact of the misleading arguments presented in the podcast.
Therefore, future studies investigating the effects of AIgenerated audio could incorporate manipulations of topic complexity and speaker characteristics (such as likeability).

A related question is whether the misinformation effects observed here depend on any features specific to AI generation, rather than reflecting effects of persuasive misinformation more generally, which the current study could not address.

However, direct comparisons of AI-and human-generated text have largely found them to be similarly persuasive (Hölbling et al., 2025; see also Goldstein et al., 2024), suggesting that the distinctive risk of generative AI lies not in a persuasive advantage but the scale and accessibility of content production.
text.formatted: However, direct comparisons of AI-and human-generated text have largely found them to be similarly persuasive <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hölbling et al., 2025</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Goldstein et al., 2024)</ref>, suggesting that the distinctive risk of generative AI lies not in a persuasive advantage but the scale and accessibility of content production.

text.text: Furthermore, while AI-generated content can be seen as lower in source credibility than human-generated content (Ji & Zhang, 2026) (given the direction of effects) that AI trust may be more resistant to inoculation when recipients have more AI experience (and are older).
text.formatted: Furthermore, while AI-generated content can be seen as lower in source credibility than human-generated content <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Ji & Zhang, 2026)</ref> (given the direction of effects) that AI trust may be more resistant to inoculation when recipients have more AI experience (and are older).

text.text: One possible explanation for this finding is that those using AI more often have experienced greater benefit from the technology, hence fostering a more forgiving attitude towards the technology's weaknesses (Sacco et al., 2025).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for this finding is that those using AI more often have experienced greater benefit from the technology, hence fostering a more forgiving attitude towards the technology's weaknesses <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sacco et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another possibility is that more-experienced AI users have greater confidence in their ability to navigate the potential risks associated with using AI (Said et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Another possibility is that more-experienced AI users have greater confidence in their ability to navigate the potential risks associated with using AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Said et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, passive and active inoculations only significantly reduced misinformation beliefs in Experiment 1 when excluding participants with previous NotebookLM experience from the AI-podcast condition, suggesting that the impact of misleading information from an AI-generated podcast may be diminished by familiarity with the tool used-though not consistently, given the lack of replication in Experiment 2.
A reason for this finding could lie in the (unchangeable) podcast voices used by NotebookLM.

Recognizing the distinct voices may have acted as a "soft" inoculation to those who had experience with NotebookLM, as they would have found the synthetic nature of the AI podcast more salient or have some insight into how the AI podcast was produced; this may, in turn, have reduced the perceived credibility of the conveyed information.

Alternatively, familiar individuals may have simply found the podcast less engaging, potentially resulting in a weaker effect of the persuasive narrative techniques (Braddock & Dillard, 2016; Lindgren, 2022 Lindgren, , 2023;; Nee & Santana, 2022; Shen et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Alternatively, familiar individuals may have simply found the podcast less engaging, potentially resulting in a weaker effect of the persuasive narrative techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Braddock & Dillard, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Lindgren, 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Lindgren, , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Nee & Santana, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Shen et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Against previous theorising (McGuire & Papageorgis, 1961; Tyler et al., 1979) and findings (M. Green et al., 2022; McIlhiney et al., 2026), we found no evidence that active inoculation was more effective than passive inoculation; in fact, passive inoculation most consistently reduced general AI trust.
text.formatted: Against previous theorising <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(McGuire & Papageorgis, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Tyler et al., 1979)</ref> and findings (M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Green et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">McIlhiney et al., 2026)</ref>, we found no evidence that active inoculation was more effective than passive inoculation; in fact, passive inoculation most consistently reduced general AI trust.

text.text: Thus, it is possible that active inoculation imparts no advantage for misinformation in the audio modality.
However, a more likely explanation is that the distinction between passive and active inoculation was less distinct in the current study than extant work.

That is, unlike previous studies, the passive inoculation may have fostered engagement by providing explicit examples of how nefarious actors can use AI tools to generate a misleading article and convert it to podcast audio.

The active component in Experiment 1 arguably required only a minimal level of additional engagement, with participants selecting from predefined AI chat prompts; however, expanding this in Experiment 2 by giving participants agency over the argument and manipulation technique used in the explicit example provided similar outcomes.

Consequently, it may either be sufficient to simply provide relevant examples for a maximized inoculation effect, or greater engagement is required in the active component to produce greater impact (Tyler et al., 1979).
text.formatted: Consequently, it may either be sufficient to simply provide relevant examples for a maximized inoculation effect, or greater engagement is required in the active component to produce greater impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Tyler et al., 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should thus seek to find optimized protocols for passive and active inoculations.
Such research could, for example, investigate an active component that involves direct interaction with an AI agent (as in Costello et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Such research could, for example, investigate an active component that involves direct interaction with an AI agent (as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Costello et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: There were some additional limitations.

First, we drew our sample from the US only, potentially introducing the confound of differences in AI trust and usage due to culture (Cvetkovic et al., 2026; Dang & Li, 2025; Epstein et al., 2023; Gillespie et al., 2023).
text.formatted: First, we drew our sample from the US only, potentially introducing the confound of differences in AI trust and usage due to culture <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cvetkovic et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dang & Li, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Epstein et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Gillespie et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies may thus seek to incorporate culturally diverse samples to investigate interventions for AI-generated misinformation.
Further, participants in the present study were simply provided with AI-generated materials, rather than interacting with an AI system directly.
Therefore, it is unclear how effective an AI-source-focused inoculation may be in the context of direct dialogue with an AI chatbot-creating a potential avenue for future research.
In conclusion, this study demonstrates that misinformation delivered through an AIgenerated audio podcast can influence people's beliefs.

Pre-emptive AI-source-focused inoculation interventions reduced both general trust in AI-generated information and endorsement of specific AI-generated misinformation, highlighting their promise as a countermeasure across audio and written formats (McIlhiney et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Pre-emptive AI-source-focused inoculation interventions reduced both general trust in AI-generated information and endorsement of specific AI-generated misinformation, highlighting their promise as a countermeasure across audio and written formats <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McIlhiney et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, inoculation effects were partly contingent on controlling for prior experience with AI, and the interventions did not fully eliminate misinformation effects on relevant beliefs.
Findings thus underscore the persistent influence of AI-generated misinformation and reinforce ongoing concerns about its impact.
